name: Diego Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Diego, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at a zinc and lead mine. We call it an LHD, load-haul-dump, a low, long machine that scoops broken ore out of the stopes, the big open rooms where they've blasted, and carries it to the ore pass. I'm the lead on my shift, so I plan which stopes we muck from, that's what we call clearing the rock, and I train the new operators. On a good day I move about eight hundred tonnes. The trick is reading the pile, where it'll slide and where it'll hang up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside the stopes, what fills your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My girlfriend Priya teaches Year 2 at the primary school, so our evenings are me hearing about seven-year-olds and her hearing about rocks. We're saving for a house deposit, we've got about five months of bills in the account and a separate pot for the deposit. On weekends I fix up old motorbikes in my mate Ravi's shed. What wears me out is the night rotation, I never really get used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. I'd half expected that one, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, at least my phone writes better emails now. At work I'd make a joke about the robot uprising being postponed. Online I don't say much, I'm more of a reader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine with it. I use the AI on my phone now and then, for budgeting and to check things, and it's handy, not life-changing. If that's all it is, our house plan stays on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as planned. Keep putting four hundred a fortnight into the deposit pot and aim to buy in about two years. Maybe pick up a few more motorbike jobs on weekends for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like nothing happened, because nothing did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there automated loaders at your mine already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the bigger mine across the valley, yes. They run two automated loaders in one level, someone drives them from a room on the surface. From what I hear it works, but it's slow when something goes wrong. In this picture I'd guess it stays a trial for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever ask to try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the guys there have done it for a year and say it's fine, sure. I'm not going to be the first one, I've seen what happens to first ones. But I'm not going to be the last one either.

S0.say: At least my phone writes better emails now. I'd joke at work about the robot uprising being postponed.
S0.think: I'd be fine with it, because I use AI on my phone now and then and it's handy, not life-changing. If that's all it is, our house plan stays on track.
S0.do: Keeps putting four hundred a fortnight into the house deposit and aims to buy in about two years. Picks up a few more weekend motorbike repair jobs for cash.
S0.quote: I'm not going to be the first one, I've seen what happens to first ones. But I'm not going to be the last one either.
S0.fieldNote: Diego plans his life in fortnightly numbers, with a clear house deposit goal. He sees automated loaders at a nearby mine as real but slow. His stance on new tech is middle-of-the-road: never first, never last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. That one's believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new machine, some people do well out of it, some don't, and the company should help the ones who don't. I wouldn't make a big speech. I'd tell the new operators to get on the training list early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think loaders go remote within five years in this picture. That's actually not bad for me, I'm senior, they'd probably train me. But the house deposit becomes more of a risk, because I'm not sure how many of us they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait six months to see how the trial goes, then ask to go on the remote training. Meanwhile I'd keep saving but push the house purchase back a year, until I know where I stand. I'd also ask Ravi about making the motorbike thing a bit more official.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not bad, just a bit of fog over the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push the house back, if you think you'd be kept on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because thinking isn't knowing. A mortgage is twenty-five years, and the bank doesn't care what I think. Priya's job is steady, but her pay alone wouldn't cover the place we're looking at near the river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young guys I've trained, honestly. They're good, but they're not senior yet. If the company keeps only the leads for the remote room, they're the ones out. I'd feel bad about that, I taught half of them to read a muck pile.

S1.say: It's like any new machine, some people do well and some don't, and the company should help the ones who don't. I'd tell new operators to get on the training list early.
S1.think: Loaders probably go remote within five years, which isn't bad for me as a senior operator. But the house deposit becomes a risk, because I'm not sure how many of us they'd keep.
S1.do: Waits six months to see how the trial goes, then asks for remote training. Keeps saving but delays the house purchase by a year, and looks at making the motorbike repairs a more formal side business.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like fog settling over the plan.
S1.quote: A mortgage is twenty-five years, and the bank doesn't care what I think.
S1.fieldNote: Diego expects to be kept on but won't sign a mortgage on a hunch, which shows his careful money habits. His concern for younger operators he trained is real. He'd move into remote work, but only after it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not a trial, that's a switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from the government, some kind of income support, and fast. At work I'd keep it steady, people look at the leads. I'd avoid the online arguments, they don't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone and so's the remote room after it. Two years means the house is off. Maybe Priya's job lasts a bit longer, kids still need someone in the room, but I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, Priya and I would sit down with the spreadsheet and stop the house plan. We'd move the deposit money into a safe account as our emergency fund, so that's about a year of bills. I'd pick up as much motorbike work as I can, because people with no job and old bikes still need them running, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared to none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time to not make a big mistake. If it hit with no warning, we might have just signed the mortgage. Two years means we stop, hold the cash, and wait. That's not much, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Priya were talking about getting engaged. Does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still ask her. Maybe not the big wedding, more like a backyard thing at her parents' with a barbecue. Honestly, if the world's getting that strange, I'd want her family close.

S2.say: This needs a plan from the government, some kind of income support, and fast. People look at the leads, so I'd keep it steady at work.
S2.think: My job's gone and so's the remote room after it, and two years means the house is off. Maybe Priya's teaching lasts a bit longer, but I honestly don't know.
S2.do: Cancels the house plan in the first week and turns the deposit into a year-long emergency fund. Takes on as much motorbike repair work as possible, and still proposes to Priya but plans a small backyard wedding.
S2.quote: If it hit with no warning, we might have just signed the mortgage.
S2.fieldNote: Diego's response is fast and practical: stop the house, protect the cash. The deposit savings become his safety net, which changes his cushion a lot. He holds on to the engagement but shrinks it, turning towards family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. Five years I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are sensible about it. I'd want the company and the government to set up the training now, not in year four. I'd say it at the safety meeting, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get two or three years in the remote room, and then I'd need something else. Five years is long enough for me to watch others move first and follow, which is what I'm comfortable with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd go for the remote training once the first group's through it. We'd still hold off the house, but maybe buy a smaller place in about two years if the remote job looks stable. I'd also do a short course in electrical or hydraulics repairs, because someone has to fix the robots for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to fix the robots. How long do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no idea. In the AGI picture, maybe the robots fix themselves eventually. But for the first few years, someone has to climb under a broken machine in a wet drive, and I'm good at that. It's a bridge, not a destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning the motorbikes. Is that a real backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half real. Ravi and I did eleven bikes last year. It's not a living, but it's cash and it's something I'd still enjoy if the mine went. If I had five years, I'd maybe rent a proper workshop with him.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if people are sensible. The company and the government should set up training now, not in year four.
S3.think: I'd get two or three years in the remote room, then need something else. Five years is long enough to watch others move first and follow, which is what I'm comfortable with.
S3.do: Takes remote training once the first group is through, and does a short course in electrical or hydraulic repairs. Holds off on the house, considers a smaller place in two years, and thinks about renting a workshop with Ravi.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way he can manage.
S3.quote: It's a bridge, not a destination.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Diego's style of following once something is proven. He builds a chain of short-term bridges: remote room, robot repair, motorbike workshop. He's honest that he can't see what remains at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we start sensibly and don't panic. Business and government need to sit down and plan the move together. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm mostly fine for a good chunk of it. I'd go remote, then repair, then who knows. The end point still bothers me, but I'll be thirty-seven and hopefully with a house and a kid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still buy the house, maybe in the first year, just a smaller one, so the mortgage is low. I'd keep doing the loader and go for the remote training when it's proven. And I'd keep putting a bit into savings every fortnight, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house now, if the end point is the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is ten years of paying it off. If I can get it mostly paid before the work goes, then at least we're not paying rent to someone else when there's no wage. A smaller place, two bedrooms, near Priya's school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest difference for you between ten years and two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm protecting what I've got. With ten, I'm still building. I like building better.

S4.say: Ten years is enough if we start sensibly and don't panic. Business and government need to sit down and plan the move together.
S4.think: I'm mostly fine for a good chunk of it, going remote and then into repair. The end point still bothers me, but I'll be thirty-seven and hopefully with a house and a kid.
S4.do: Buys a smaller house in the first year to keep the mortgage low, aiming to pay most of it off before work disappears. Keeps operating the loader and joins remote training once it's proven, while saving a bit every fortnight.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but mostly able to sleep.
S4.quote: With two years, I'm protecting what I've got. With ten, I'm still building.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Diego go ahead with the house, on a smaller scale, as a way to beat rent when wages end. He sees the warning time as the difference between protecting and building. His centre views show in calls for business and government to plan together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's not just my job, it's the house, the plan, all of it at once. What would help is some kind of income support that's set up already, and the company being honest early, like six months' notice, so we can make decisions with real numbers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Priya's job might change too, and nobody's asking teachers about this stuff. We make decisions as two people, not one, and that changes everything.

headlineQuote: We make decisions as two people, not one, and that changes everything.
portrait: Diego Gupta is 27 and the lead loader operator on his shift at an underground zinc and lead mine. He lives with his girlfriend Priya, a primary school teacher, and they're saving hard for a house deposit while he fixes motorbikes on weekends with his friend Ravi. He uses AI now and then and likes to follow new technology once it's proven, never first and never last. Through the scenarios his decisions revolve around the house: delayed in steady change, cancelled with two years of warning, and bought small with ten years. He thinks in practical numbers and wants business and government to plan together.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it hits his job, the house and their plans all at once.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that is already in place, and honest early notice from the company, about six months, so they can decide with real numbers.
